author: reek
body: A runnable model of raymarched volumetric clouds. A ray goes in, a scattered colour and a transmittance come out. This is the simulation a cloud shader evaluates per pixel, written so it can be executed and checked rather than only rendered.

author: reek
body: It cites `OceanModel` for the Real math kernel and `V3`. That chapter was made a library with no entry point precisely so the next wave could do this, and the pieces reused are the general ones -- range-reduced sine, Newton sqrt, saturate, the vector algebra. Nothing about waves is used here; whole-program dead-code elimination drops it.

author: reek
body: One piece the ocean did not need had to be built: an **exponential**. Beer's law is an exponential and nothing else, and the foreword's near-zero approximations are useless for optical depths that run to tens. `c-exp` is range-reduced the same way `w-sin` is, for the same reason.

author: reek
body: exp(x) = 2^k * exp(r), choosing k so the remainder r lands in [-ln2/2, ln2/2]. Over that interval eight Taylor terms are exact to better than one part in a hundred million, which is far below anything a transmittance can carry.

author: reek
body: The clamp is not decoration. `w-trunc` converts through `real-to-int`, so an unbounded argument would convert a value no Integer can hold. It is also physically right: exp(-80) is 1.8e-35, and a transmittance that small is zero against any colour it will multiply.

author: reek
body: A lattice noise: hash the eight integer corners of the cell a point falls in, then interpolate with a quintic fade.

author: reek
body: The final scale is a multiply by the reciprocal for the same reason. A divide by a constant on this path is a divide per corner per octave.

author: reek
body: The fractal sum. Each octave doubles the frequency and halves the amplitude, and the total is divided by the amplitude sum so the result stays in [0,1] however many octaves are asked for.

author: reek
body: `c-remap` is the workhorse: it rescales a value from one interval to another and is how coverage and erosion are applied without a branch. Raising coverage lowers the floor of the remap, so more of the noise range survives into the cloud.

author: reek
body: The height gradient is what makes a cloud read as a cloud rather than as noise in a box. Cumulus are dense and rounded underneath, where rising air is still saturated, and frayed on top where it has mixed with dry air above. So density ramps up quickly over the bottom fifth of the slab and falls away across the top third.

author: reek
body: The density at a point. The base shape is a low-octave fractal remapped by coverage and shaped by the gradient; the detail sum then erodes it from below, which is what carves the cauliflower edges. Erosion is weighted toward the top of the slab, because that is where the mixing that frays a cloud actually happens.

author: reek
body: `2 * beer * powder` is the combined form; the factor of two restores the mid-range that the product would otherwise halve.

author: reek
body: The 1.5 power is a square root of a cube rather than a general power, which the kernel does not have and does not need.

author: reek
body: Two nested marches. The view ray steps through the slab accumulating scattered light and attenuating transmittance; at every step that holds density, a shorter march toward the sun measures how much sunlight reached that point.

author: reek
body: The light march is the expensive part and the reason a cloud shader is costly. It is also why it is deliberately short: six steps over a lengthening stride, which resolves the self-shadowing that matters and nothing finer.

author: reek
body: The accumulator. `trans` is how much of the background still shows through; `r`,`g`,`b` are the scattered light gathered so far. They are kept as scalars rather than a `V3` on purpose: the march allocates one record per step either way, and this keeps that to one instead of several on a path that runs tens of times per pixel and has no garbage collector under it.

author: reek
body: One step. Below the density floor the step contributes nothing and only costs a density lookup, which is the usual case for most of a ray.

author: reek
body: `c-exp` is evaluated once and used twice. It is the most expensive call in the model and this loop is its hottest caller.

author: reek
body: The view march. It stops early when the ray is effectively opaque, which is the single biggest saving in the whole model: a ray that has entered a dense cumulus has nothing left to learn from the far side of it.

author: reek
body: The sample sits at `t + step * jitter`, and the caller varies `jitter` per ray. With a fixed offset every ray in the frame samples the volume on the same set of planes, and where those planes cut a cloud they draw visible bands across it -- the single most recognisable artifact a raymarcher has, and one that no amount of extra steps removes, because more steps only makes the bands finer and keeps them coherent. Decorrelating the offset between neighbouring rays trades that structured error for unstructured noise, which the eye reads as texture instead of as a mistake. It is the same reasoning behind a dither pattern and it costs one hash.

author: reek
body: Where the ray enters and leaves the slab. A ray climbing or descending crosses both planes; one running level through the slab never leaves it, and one that misses entirely gets an empty interval.

author: reek
body: The whole model, for one ray. `jitter` is where in each step the sample is taken, in [0,1); see the note above `c-view-march`.

author: reek
body: The midpoint rule, for a single ray asked about on its own. A driver sampling a handful of directions wants the unbiased answer, not a decorrelated one.

author: reek
body: The coordinates are scrambled before they reach the hash, and passing the raw `x` and `y` is not good enough. `c-hash3` begins by combining its three arguments LINEARLY, so neighbouring pixels enter the mixer a fixed distance apart and leave it correlated; the offsets then vary smoothly across the screen instead of independently, and the bands the jitter is meant to break up come back as a cross-hatch. Feeding it three quantities that each depend on both x and y, with unrelated multipliers, is what actually decorrelates neighbours.

author: reek
body: The slab, in metres above the viewer.

author: reek
body: Shape. The base frequency sets how large a single cumulus is; the detail frequency sets how fine its edges are.

author: reek
body: Coverage is the single most expressive dial: 0.35 gives scattered fair weather cumulus, 0.7 an overcast deck.

author: reek
body: The multiple-scattering floor. See the note above c-march-step.

author: reek
body: Its colour is NOT the sky colour, which was the first thing tried and is wrong in a way that shows: tinting the floor with deep sky blue makes even the sunlit face of a cloud come out blue-dominant, because the floor is a large fraction of the total. Light that has bounced several times inside a cloud has been scattered by water droplets, which are near-neutral, so what fills the shadows is mostly the cloud's own light and only a little sky.

author: reek
body: Where the view march gives up. A ray that has lost 96% of its transmittance has nothing left to learn from the far side of the cloud it is inside, and the remaining steps are the most expensive ones in the frame because they are the ones that run the light march. Raising this from 0.01 to 0.04 is invisible in the image and removes a large slice of the work.

author: reek
body: This chapter is a library and carries no entry point, for the same reason `OceanModel` carries none: a chapter with an `opening` cannot be cited by a program that has its own.

author: reek
body: `CloudSamples` marches a few rays and prints what came back. `CloudRender` draws the sky as an image.
